MONTREAL 


Poung Mens Christian Association. 


27TH ANNUAL REPORT 
Submitted on Tuesday Evening, November 26th, 1878. 


—___—_—_-¢@>- ___ 


We cannot commence to detail the work of the past year, 
without acknowledging, with a deep sense of gratitude to God, 
the wisdom and grace and strength which He has so liberally laid 
to the hands of His servants in the prosecution of this work. 
While endeavoring to persuade young men of the true liberty 
which is only to be found in Christ Jesus,—while trying to rescue 
the perishing and fallen,—while visiting the sick, and while com- 
muning together over His revealed Word in order to gain strength 
for the journey, the many rich blessings have all been ours, and 
the glory and the honor we ascribe to Him. 


By no means the least of these blessings has been the 
delightful christian intercourse and fellowship which the members 
have enjoyed, for while representing different branches of the 
Church on earth, these distinctions have all been lost when 
gathered around the person of our Great Head and realizing our 
oneness in Him. 


We desire to offer special thanksgiving for the removal of 
one great burden which for some years has weighed so heavily 
upon the workers and the work—the debt upon the Building of 
$18,000. The kind and generous offer of Mr. McLachlan at the 
last Annual Meeting was accepted, and before April the response 
from the young men had been so noble that, notwithstanding 
the “hard times,” the $10,000 allotted to them was subscribed. 
The' Merchants were not slow in appreciating the self-denying 
efforts of the members, and subscriptions were promised to Mr. 
McLachlan nearly covering the balance. These payments ex- 
tend over a period of three years, and it is most gratifying to record 


SSS = 


a ae 


—— 


6 


the promptness with which they have been met, although 
in many cases calling forth the greatest self-denial on the part of 
the donors. A special meeting was held in April, to which all 
were invited who had subscribed towards the removal of this debt, 
and those present will not readily forget the cheering testimonies 
given by many who confessed their indebtedness to the Associa- 
tion to an extent which in this life they would never be able to 
repay. 

We look forward with joy and confidence to the speedy 
realization of our hopes—a Building dedicated for christian work, 
for the young men of Montreal, free of debt. Surely it is not too 
much to ask from the christians of this city, considering that there 
are 356 licensed and 118 unlicensed saloons and Billiard Rooms, 
besides Club Houses and other avenues to death, open day and 
night, where hundreds of our noblest young men are continually 
being sacrificed on the altar of sin and vice, and are lost to 
society, to the world, and to God. 


. 


— . ~e> 


REPORTS FROM SUB-COMMITTEES. 


DEVOTIONAL MEETINGS. 


During the year 617 religious services have been held in the 
Building, with an estimated total attendance of 37,376. Fourteen 
regular Weekly Meetings have been held, besides Special Meetings, 
and considered altogether, they have been characterized by 
interest, pleasure, and profit to all concerned. Individual testi- 
monies have been frequently given in acknowledgment of blessings, 
and we have the assurance that many young men have been 
directed into the narrow way which leadeth to life eternal. 


The Daily Prayer Meeting has had a fluctuating attendance. 
During the Summer months the number is small, but in the Fall 
and Winter the average is greatly increased. . ‘Through this means 
of grace a change has been produced in the life of many a man, 
while disheartened and depressed by surrounding circumstances, 
and many of God’s children have experienced it to be an oasis in 


7 


the desert, where they have “ with joy drawn water from the wells 
of Salvation,” and increased their courage and strength by obey- 
ing the command—“ Wait on the Lord, be of good courage and 
he shall strengthen thine heart.” The special Thanksgiving 
Service on Christmas morning when those added to the Church 
during the year confessed their allegiance to Christ will not soon 


be forgotten. 


Young Men’s Evangelistic Meeting.—This ever continues to 
be a joyful reunion of those engaged in the arduous work of the 
week. The attendance is from 60 to 100 every Saturday evening 
and the practical results leave no room to doubt as to the 
blessing which follows this service. At the close of a recent 
meeting a young student came forward to join the Association, 
and stated that at one of the meetings last year he had been 
awakened from a careless, sinful life, and was now rejoicing 
in the liberty to be found in Christ. A German young man 
who for some years had given himself over to scepticism and 
infidelity, through this meeting was aroused to the power of the 
Gospel, and is now a humble follower of the Lord Jesus Christ. 
Instances might be continued did space permit. 


Evangelistic Bible Class.—This is held every Sunday after- 
noon under the direction of the Secretary. The average atten- 
dance is 35. As soon as a young man becomes interested in the 
study of the scriptures, he is drafted into some Sabbath-School as 
teacher ; no less than four teachers and one librarian have been 
taken from this class during the past year. Visitors to the city 
increase the attendance during the summer months. 


Tuesday Evening Class for Bible Study is now under the 
leadership of Mr. W. L. Fraser, who accepted the position on 
the resignation of Mr. Alf. Sandham, he being called from the 
city to. labor in connection with the Methodist Church. Some 
time previous to his departure the class presented him with a very 
handsome Bible. The attendance which numbers about 20 is 
chiefly composed of christian young men, and the study of the 
epistle to the Romans is full of interest. This class is conversa- 
tional in its character. 


Service of Song.—This has recently been started on Tuesday 
evenings from 9 to 10, and with much acceptance. The object 


8 


is to become more familiar with the singing of the Gospel Songs, 
and under the leadership of Mr. Coates is being accomplished. 
It is open to ladies as well as gentlemen. 


The Gospel Temperance Meeting has been held every Sunday 
afternoon but with varying interest. At present it is being con- 
ducted with vigor and earnestness, and the attendance has largely 
increased. Short addresses are given by clergymen and others, 
and an opportunity is afforded to sign the pledge. 


The Sunday Evening Evangelistic Meeting 1s always as 
largely attended as the Hall will permit. The attention given is 
good, and the seed of the word has been sown by loving hearts and 
willing hands. The addresses are short and pointed, and the 
meeting is closed promptly at 9.30. A Prayer Meeting is held at 
the close, and seldom without ‘“ enquirers.” These are followed 
up, and introduced to the Churches, and in many cases we are 
permitted to see the results. Our prayer is that God may make 
us wise in winning souls. 


The Boys Meeting, although attended by those young in 
years is none the less important, as it is much easier for the 
youthful heart to receive the Gospel truths than after evil associa- 
2 | tion and habits have worked their hardening effect upon the life. 
) oe Jesus says: “verily I say unto you except ye be converted and 
become as a little child ye shall not enter into the kingdom of 
heaven.”—-Mat. 18-3. They meet every Friday evening, and the 
Chairman reports that although the average attendance has not 
( been very large this year, they are encouraged in seeing a more 
active interest manifested, and have reason to believe that con- 
i versions have resulted. Some parents: object to have their boys 
i going out alone, but the workers will call at any address which 
parents will send to the Secretary. The Chairman selects a sub- 
I ject such as “Blood,” “ Peace,” ‘‘ Trust,” &c., and they are 
k requested to bring passages bearing upon it, and in this way they 
if become instructed in the truths of God’s Word. Invitation slips 
i, containing scripture texts, have been circulated by the workers 
| amongst their companions. Special prayer is asked on behalf of 
| this meeting. A branch has lately been commenced at 30 Fort 
Street on the same evening. | 


9 


In connection with the “‘ Week of Prayer for young men,” 
sermons were preached from fifteen of the city pulpits, and the 
daily meetings were characterized with unusual earnestness. 


The duty of hospitality is yearly laid upon the Association, 
in extending christian courtesies to visiting brethren from all 
parts of the world. Prominent amongst them was Major Malan 
of London, Eng., formerly a worker in the Association. He 
addressed the meetings on many occasions, and the word was 
always with power. Previous to his departure a very happy 
re-union was held in the Rooms, when as many as possible of the 
old members and workers were gathered together, and listened to 
an earnest farewell address from their esteemed Brother in the 
Lord. More recently, Dr. W. P. Mackay of Hull, Eng., most 
favorably known to many of our members as the author of *‘ Grace 
and Truth.” Although here but a short time his powerful ad- 
dresses awakened a deep interest in many hearts. 

In the department of Lectures the Committee have arranged 
for a weekly course extending throughout the winter months, 
These are free to members and their friends, and are contributed 
by men whose names are sufficient guarantee as to the character of 
the addresses. It is believed that this will supply a want in the pro- 
gramme of the Association which has long been felt and expressed. 

The following statement will show the attendance at the 


various meetings :—

MISSION MEETINGS. | 


‘‘ Sown in the darkness, or sown in the light, 
Sown in our weakness, or sown in our might, 
Gathered in time or eternity 7 
Sure, oh sure, will the harvest be.” 
Probably at no period in the history of the Association has 
the work of this Committee been so vigorously prosecuted as 


B 


10 


during the past winter under the supervision of Mr. Hy. Sandham 
assisted by a faithful band of over fifty members. As the report 
shows earnest and faithful work has been done in the by-ways and 
outskirts of the city, where the Gospel message has been carried 
by willing hearts. The organization meeting held at the Chair- 
man’s house in November last, gave clear indication of the bles- 
sing which accompanied both the workers and the work. A 
monthly Plan is issued, giving the appointments for every mem- 
ber, and he is expected either to be present himself or in the 
person of a substitute. Conversions have been reported from 
several of the meetings, and in each locality they have been 
characterized with more or less religious interest. In March last 
a hall was secured on Chatham and services held every Sunday 
evening until May. Special interest was manifested, and if faith- 
fully carried on, this will doubtless become a most important 
mission. The money expended in this work has been $65— 


contributed by the workers themselves. ‘The benefit from this 


work as a means of training young men for useful active member- 
ship in the Church of Christ, should not be undervalued. 


The following carefully tabulated statement contains the 
facts of this work. It will be seen that 405 meetings have been 
held with a total attendance of 7236. With one or two exceptions | 
the services are only held for six months.

FINANCE COMMITTEE. 


The depression in Trade has not been without its influence 
upon the finances of the Association, causing some of its supporters 
to withdraw their subscriptions and others to considerably reduce 
the amount which they usually gave, yet we gratefully recognise 
the liberality of many of the members of the Association and a 
number of the merchants of the city, who have most generously 
responded to the appeal made at the beginning of the year, to clear 
off the debt which has been permitted too long to cumber and 
embarrass the usefulness of the Association. In response to the 
appeal, the Young Men have subscribed $9,145.00, of which 
amount $2,768.31 has been paid to date, and in addition to this 
we have the amount collected or promised by Mr. John S. 
McLachlan, who, in the most generous manner, promised to raise 
$10,000 or half the amount requisite to place the Association free 
from debt. It will thus be seen that at a very early date we have 
good hope of seeing the Association clear of debt and able, with 
greater vigour than ever, to undertake and carry out work for 
the blessed Master. ‘Through Mr. Mclachlan’s efforts, a sum of 
#200 sterling has been subscribed and paid towards the building 
debt in Great Britain, which sum we desire thankfully to acknow- 
ledge here. 


A Note for $5,000 which has been kept floating for years 
we have been able to pay off this year, together with a sum 
of $500 towards a claim of Mr. Hutchison for $750.00, an 
amount long due and which should have been settled years ago. 
We regret to say an old account for the Christian Worker has 
turned up quite unexpectedly, which account however we hope to 
settle upon a satisfactory basis in a few days. Appended we give a 
list of those gentlemen who have so liberally responded to the 
appeal to wipe out the debt, and we shall have great pleasure in 
adding to the list any member’s name who has not yet availed 

himself of this opportunity to do good. 


At the earliest opportunity, a body of Sustaining Members 
should be raised who would agree to give annually say a sum of 
$5.00 and thus afford to the Finance Committee a regular and 
assured source of income, and when the debt is finally removed, 
upon this body could then easily rest the honor and work of sus- 


12 


taining the Association in financial strength—making the labors 
of the Finance Committee comparatively light and the duties ‘of 
the Treasurer a positive pleasure.

DISTRIBUTION OF RELIGIOUS READING. 


This Department has been extensively carried on during the 
past year. Every Sabbath morning a band of the Members have 
visited all the ships in the Harbor, and distributed tracts in the 
different languages. ‘They are always gladly welcomed by the 
men in the forecastle, and opportunities constantly afforded for 
religious conversation. At times they are permitted to read a 
portion of God’s word, and the seed thus sown in faith will doubt- 
less be gathered in the “ bundle of life.” One bright English lad, 
who had been converted while at our meetings during the summer, 
gave the most cheering evidence of his growth in grace, and of 
God’s ability to sustain his children even amidst the temptations 
which beset a sailor’s life. Another young man who had been 
converted at meetings conducted by Miss Macpherson’s workers 
amongst the thieves in East London, gave evidence of the Spirit’s 
power and seemed to be much blessed during his sojourn here. 
The services at the Sailor’s Institute, under the supervision of 
Mr. John Ritchie have been more largely attended. These kind- 
hearted noble sailors need the sympathy and prayers of the 
christian people to a greater extent than they receive. 


The work of this Committee amongst the Firemen has been 
faithfully carried on, over 5,500 books, papers and tracts, being 
distributed amongst them. Their reception by the whole Brigade 
is most cordial, and opportunities are taken to impress upon these 
men, whose lives are in such constant danger, the necessity of 


nH 
it 


14 


eternal life in Christ. Two meetings have been held weekly in 
the stations, with a fair attendance. During the sickness and 
death of one of the “ guardians,” some of the workers constantly 
visited him, and this visitation is carried on whenever any of the 
men are laid aside through injury or sickness. Special prayer is 
asked for this work. Religious Magazines and papers are greatly 
needed, and contributions of such will be thankfully received. 


House-to-house visitation has been commenced in some 
sections of the East End, especially in that locality known as the 
haunts of the “ Black Horse Gang,” and the workers are encou- 
raged. They endeavor to take the children to Sabbath-School, 
and in this way, perhaps reach the parents. 


READING ROOM AND LIBRARY. 


The daily attendance of readers and visitors is even an in- 
crease on the previous year, which was over go,ooo. Although it 
is free to all, we have not had that difficulty in dealing with the 
“Tramp nuisance,” experienced by many Associations which 1s 
such a hindrance to their usefulness. In order to advertise our 
Association and its work more fully, large cards were printed, 
containing list of our meetings and a register of Church Services, 
which have been placed in the principal hotels and public places. 


The list of papers and magazines on file in the Reading Room

London e 

The Circulating Library has been used but little, only 730 
volumes having been drawn from it during the year, and if we 
are to retain a class of our membership it should be replenished 
with the modern literature. The retiring Committee suggest that 
a monthly allowance be placed at the disposal of their successors 
for this purpose. 


16 


The Reference Library has been greatly used, but it also 
needs the addition of modern works of reference, which are 
constantly asked for. | 


In December last an auction sale was held of the papers and 
magazines received at the Rooms, the purchaser getting posses- 
sion of the old number as soon as the new one was received. It 
being the first sale held by the Association, it was not understood 
by many, but the result was satisfactory. The Committee would 
recommend its being repeated. ) 


MEMBERSHIP COMMITTEE. 


With the last report our membership was in a most unsatis- 
factory condition. During the year a careful and thorough revision 
has been made, and the list as it now stands shows the actual 
strength of the Association. ‘he “subscribers ” comprise those 
who contribute more than the annual fee, and are given separate 
from the ordinary members. We have received an addition of 
go new members. Thirty-one have left the city and eight have 
died. 


Active Members,.:......... 275 
Associate Members.......... 213

785 


RECEPTION COMMITTEE. 


The work of this Committee has been to have one or more 
of its members in attendance each evening in order to welcome 
strangers and show the members every attention, making the 
Rooms as attractive and social as possible. This is an impor- 
tant work, as the desire for fellowship and companionship is one 
of the strongest instincts of the human nature, and the first im- 
pression which a young man receives may be the turning point in 
his life. The attendance varies from 20 to 40 or 50, and oppor- 
tunities are offered and accepted of speaking to young men about 
their soul’s salvation. It is hoped in the future to establish a 
regular prayer meeting at 9.30, but this has not been carried out 


17 


continuously throughout the past year, on account of the difficulty 
of securing a chairman. 


INVITATION COMMITEE. 


This Committee meets every Saturday evening, and after 
prayer go forth two by two and visit the Hotels, Billiard Saloons, 
and some are stationed on the corners of leading thouroughfares 
to distribute invitations to the Young Men’s Meeting. There has 
been a weekly average attendance of 9 workers, and over 40,000 
invitations (on each of which there are scripture texts) have been 
distributed. Invitations have also been distributed on Sunday 
to the Bible Class and Temperance Meeting. The managers of 
the Windsor cheerfully consented to members of our Committee 
visiting their Hotel. ‘The workers often meet with many insults 
and rebuffs while on this duty, but they are borne patiently. The 
Chairman adds that it 1s with very grateful hearts that they testify 
to the blessing received personally through this work. One 
evening an invitation was given to a young man which read 
‘Rest—Home—Joy.’ It seemed to touch his heart, as he talked 
to the worker for a few minutes the tears flowed from his eyes. 
Young men are constantly brought in through this means and | 
induced to sign the pledge, and the result cannot be chronicled 
here. At one meeting, in response to the Chairman’s question as 
to the number who were present on account of receiving invitations, 
six young men arose and testified that they had otherwise no 
intention of being present. At a recent meeting a gentleman 
stated that he had prepared to leave for Toronto that evening, 
when he was handed one of these invitations in the Hotel. It so 
impressed him that he remained over Sunday and came to the 
meeting in order to see where such young men were educated. 


VISITATION COMMITTEE. 


This Committee visits members as well as other young men 
who may be sick. Fifteen cases (principally amongst the members) 
have claimed their attention, and these have been regularly visited. 
Words of comfort and cheer have been brought to them from Him 
of whom it is written ‘“ Himself took our infirmities and bear our 
sicknesses.” Some have been restored to health and strength 
again, and others have been called hence. 


C 


18 


While we refrain mentioning names, yet deem it to be our 
duty (having been officially connected with the Association) to 
record the death of our dear brother Horace G. Pearson, on 
September 29th, of typhoid fever, at the age of 24. Our late 
brother acted in the capacity of assistant secretary and librarian 
for a period of two years, and by his kindly manner and christian 
conversation, he won the regard and affection of the many young 
men with whom he came in contract. A most impressive funeral 
service was held in the Hall. 


A member of this Committee regularly visits the General 
Hospital, and in the nature of the case it is scarcely possible to 
give details ; the patients come and go, and are visited faithfully 
and tenderly, the seed of the kingdom being sown, and sympathy 
extended as they are able to bear it. ‘Two cases out of many 
might be named which have greatly encouraged the visitor’s heart. 


A young English Sailor left behind by his ship, gave no 
special indication that the Spirit of God had touched his heart, 
but when well and from distant parts he wrote two letters full of 
gratitude and thanksgiving to God that he had ever been taken to 
the Hospital, for there he had been born again and made a “ new 
creature ” in Christ Jesus. 


The other case—a young English Canadian had his eyes 
nearly torn out while splitting wood. More than one letter has 
been received since his return written by his mother, to express 
her own, the lads, and the family’s gratitude, for the relief and 
pleasure he received during the long weeks of enforced darkness, 
from the reading, conversation and prayer of the members of the 
Association. Although he will never again look upon God’s handi- 
work in nature, still the eyes of his faith now see as never before 
the face of one whom he can call “‘ My beloved and my friend.” 


‘* Hearts growing a weary 
With heavier woe, 

Now droop mid the darkness, 
Go, comfort them, go ! 

Go bury thy sorrows, 
Let others be blest, 

Go give them the sunshine, 
Tell Jesus the rest.” 


19 


GENERAL SECRETARY’S REPORT. 


The Secretary has endeavored to render such aid to the 
yarious Committees as the occasion required. Some have 
earnestly carried out their work almost independent of him, while 
others have allowed him to do it all. Much time was given in 
the first of the year to the prosecution of the Building Fund 
Scheme, the satisfactory result of which has been previously 
reported. 


The objects of the Association are now so well known by 
strangers as well as those in the City that the time of the 
Secretary is almost completely occupied in dealing with the 
individual cases who daily seek counsel, information, employment, 
or some other description of aid. ‘The continued and general 
depressson in business, which is experienced by no class to a 
greater extent than the young men, has greatly increased this 
general work. No less than 31 of our members have been 
compelled to leave the city for this reason, and hundreds are 
crowding here from other places in the hope of gaining some 
relief. It is sad to see men who for many years have occupied 
good positions offering their services for the merest pittance in 
order to gain food for their families. In one instance your 
Secretary found that a young man and his wife had actually gone 
without food for three days, and yet had not made known their 
circumstances. It is impossible to conceive what the suffering 
and want will be during the coming winter. 


Employment.—230 young men who could furnish satisfactory 
references, have placed their names on our Register as applicants 
for situations, and for these 48 permanent and 54 temporary 
situations have been secured. The Association does not hold 
itself responsible in this work, although the greatest care is used 
in acquainting the employer with all facts in each case. 


Correspondence-—This department has greatly increased 
during the year. From all parts of the world letters are received 
concerning young men, and also many concerning matters foreign 
toourwork. Recently aletter was received from Joppa, Palestine, 
seeking information of a young man who arrived here two years 
ago. Enquiry was made and it was ascertained that his body was 
now lying in the Cemetery, it having been found at Boucherville 


20 


in May last. ‘The result of the inquest showed that he must have 
been drowned the day after his arrival here, but the cause is still 
a mystery. Many interesting incidents might be given concerning 
the search for young men. Some found in the lowest dens of vice 
have been rescued, and in all cases the gospel is held forth as the 
only remedy by which poor fallen man can successfully conquer 
sin. ‘The number of letters written by the Secretary have been 
1,324, and 997 have been received. Over 1,200 letters have been 
written in the Rooms, material being furnished by the Association. 


Boarding Houses.—A completely revised list of boarding 
houses has been prepared, and a new plan adopted compelling 
each party registering their names to deposit 50 cents,—to be 
returned when the vacancies were filled. In this way parties 
making application for board will not be sent to houses unless 
there is a vacancy. ‘This Register is constantly used, and 
hundreds of young men who came as strangers to the City are 
furnished with suitable boarding houses. 


A Pledge Book is kept by the Secretary and signatures are 
added to it daily. During the year 307 names have been added, 
and in every case these unfortunate men are directed from this 
outward attempt at moral reform to the need of salvation through 
Christ from the power and penalty of sin. 


In coming in contact with young men at the various meetings, 
and with strangers who call at the Rooms, special care is taken to 
bring them into contact with the Pastor or same prominent mem- 
bers of the Church they attend, and in this way a double influence 
is brought to bear upon these young men. 


Letters might be given, were there space for them in this 
Report, from mothers and fathers in Canada, the States and 
England, thanking the Association for their efforts on their Son’s 
behalf. In some cases the labor appears to have been in vain ; 
in others, the evidences are most hopeful, but whatever the result 
may be, the effort has been made in the name and for the sake 
of Him who came to seek and to save the fallen and lost ones, 
and we have the assurance that it shall not return void. 


Temptations of the most deceitful and deadly nature abound 
on every side in this City. The very best of our young men, 
even those who have been most carefully reared in christian 


— 


21 


families, are falling under their power. ‘Those who have escaped 
from the “ horrible pit and the miry clay ” have to face the 
enticements of Satan’s emissaries, who are waiting and longing to 
draw them back into the ways of sin and death. ‘The young men 
who are working for the salvation of their fellow-men need the 
prayers and sympathies and support of the christian fathers and 
mothers in this City, and of all who desire to see the kingdom of 
God’s dear Son enlarged. Pray that divine wisdom may be 
youchsafed to them, and that the purifying principles of God’s 
blessed Word may have full effect in their own lives, so that they 
/ will commend the Gospel of Christ wherever they go. 


‘Unto Him who is able to keep you from falling and to 
present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceed- 
ing joy, to the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, 
dominion and power, both now and ever.— Amen.”
